newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels in Lubumbashi,pile pressure on Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels in Lubumbashi,pile pressure on Mobutu.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's rebels took control of most of Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi on Wednesday piling on pressure for embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko to quit after over three decades in power.

In Kinshasa, Mobutu named a senior general as emergency rule prime minister in a move that had all the hallmarks of a last desperate bid to reassert his dwindling authority in the capital where his army clashed with angry opposition supporters.
In Washington, the White House suggested that the time had come for the veteran African strongman, who seized power in 1965 and had prostate cancer surgery in August, to stand down.
"Mobutuism is about to become a creature of history," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, signalling the end of an alliance dating back to Cold War fears of spreading Communism.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October, control almost half of the sprawling Central African nation.
They seized the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi last week.

They entered Lubumbashi, the economically vital capital of the southern copper mining province of Shaba, on Wednesday after meeting stiff resistance from Mobutu loyalists on the approaches to the city of one million people.

"The fall of Lubumbashi is the total collapse of Mobutu because if Mobutu is intelligent he will realise that he must resign and has no other choice," Louis Nyarubasa, a rebel spokesman, said at their headquarters in Goma in the east.
After nightfall, witnesses said gunfire could still be heard in Lubumbashi and the army was reported in control of the airport six km (four miles) to the north.
A Belgian resident of the city was critically wounded by a mortar shell in his garden, expatriates said.
Mobutu, 66, decreed a nationwide state of emergency on Tuesday and sacked newly appointed prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, his arch-foe, on Wednesday.
His army clashed in Kinshasa on Wednesday with thousands of supporters of the veteran opposition leader, who was prime minister for less than a week.
Tshisekedi, his eyes streaming from the effects of teargas, tried in vain to make his way to the prime minister's office complex on foot to install his new team.
Witnesses said Mobutu's son Kongolo and other soldiers, who barred the route with armoured vehicles, escorted Tshisekedi back to his home in Kinshasa's Limete district.
Soldiers fired in the air and used teargas to disperse his supporters. Tshisekedi had a slight head wound, aides said.
"We won't take this lying down. They will find us in their path," one Tshisekedi aide said on hearing that Mobutu had appointed General Likulia Bolongo prime minister.
Likulia was defence minister in the pre-Tshisekedi administration of Kengo wa Dondo. Parliament voted out Kengo after persistent charges that he mismanaged the war.

Mobutu said in a decree that he named Likulia as Zaire's political family had withdrawn its support for Tshisekedi. Likulia was link man between Mobutu and opposition politicians at the height of pro-democracy protests between 1990 and 1992.
Tshisekedi fell foul of Mobutu supporters and allies alike after announcing a government composed of his own loyalists. He earmaked six posts for rebels, who rebuffed the offer.
Critics accuse Mobutu and his cronies of amassing fortunes while most of Zaire's 45 million people live in abject poverty in what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries.
"We are too happy, too happy. We were colonised for 35 years by that dictator Mobutu. He looted our Katanga (Shaba)," said one Lubumbashi resident Henri Kisimuzima, 48.
